# Memory in a Random Walk {#sec-memory}

In 1951, a British hydrologist published a paper in the transactions of the American Society of
Civil Engineers about how much water a reservoir should hold. The paper is 30 pages long, it has
6,272 citations according to OpenAlex [@hurst1951], and it contains an anomaly that took seventeen
years to become a mathematical object.

The anomaly is simple to state and hard to believe. If the yearly flow of a river were
independent from year to year — wet years and dry years occurring in no particular order — then the
cumulative departure of the flow from its average would grow in a specific, slow way. Hurst
looked at the records, including long series from the Nile, and found that the cumulative
departure grew faster than that.

Wet years cluster. Dry years cluster. The river remembers.

This chapter follows that observation from a practical engineering worry, through an object
invented to explain it, into a market where the object broke, and back out again into a different
field where it worked. Along the way it introduces the second half of the book's central
distinction, because the thing that broke in the market was not the memory. It was the assumption
that a model with memory can be priced with the same machinery as a model without one.

## What Brownian motion cannot do

Start with the standard model, because the anomaly is only visible against it.

A Brownian motion is a random function of time with three properties. It starts at zero. Its
increments are independent: what happens in one interval tells you nothing about the next. And its
increments are Gaussian, with a variance proportional to the length of the interval.

The third property is where the familiar square root comes from. Over a period of length n, the
typical size of the deviation is proportional to the square root of n. That is why uncertainty
about the average of a series shrinks as the square root of the sample size, and why ten thousand
observations buy you a hundredfold reduction in error.

Now consider what independence rules out. If the increments are independent, then a long run of
above-average years carries no information about the next year. In fact, a long run should be
rare, and its length should follow a simple distribution in which the probability of a run
decaying geometrically.

**Independence is not a technical convenience. It is a claim about how the world is arranged, and
the claim is that the past is uninformative.**

Hurst's data said otherwise. He described the discrepancy with a statistic — the rescaled range,
usually written R/S — which divides the range of the cumulative departures within a segment by
the standard deviation of that segment's increments. Under independence, the rescaled range should
grow as the square root of the segment length. Hurst's records grew faster.

If you write the growth rate as a power, R/S proportional to n raised to the power H, then
independence corresponds to H = 1/2, and Hurst's data gave values above it.

I am not quoting a fitted number for H from the 1951 paper, because I did not have the text, and
the value commonly attributed to it — around 0.7 — appears in the secondary literature more often
than it appears in the original record. What is checkable is the direction of the finding and the
fact that the instrument was R/S.

## Hurst's world

It helps to know what kind of document the 1951 paper is.

It appeared in the *Transactions of the American Society of Civil Engineers*, a venue for
engineering practice rather than for probability theory. Its subject was reservoir design: how much
storage does a dam need so that it does not run dry? That is an engineering question with a
capital budget attached, and it had been answered for decades by assuming that annual flows are
independent draws.

Hurst's contribution was to check the assumption against very long records, including Nile series
that extend back into the nineteenth century, and to find it wanting. He then proposed a statistic
that could be computed by an engineer with a table of numbers and no particular training in
stochastic processes.

**The instrument was designed for the audience that needed it.** That is worth noting because it
explains both the paper's influence in engineering and its invisibility to statisticians: a
rescaled-range heuristic published in an engineering transactions volume is not addressed to the
people who would eventually formalise it.

Seventeen years separate the engineering paper from the mathematical object. That gap is not
slowness. It is the distance between a profession that needs a number and a discipline that owns
the theory of such numbers.

## Two kinds of memory, and why the distinction matters

The word memory is used loosely, and the loose use causes real confusion in the applied
literature. Two quite different things get called memory.

**Short memory:** the correlation between observations decays fast enough that the sum of all
correlations converges. An autoregressive process has short memory. The past influences the
present, but its total influence is finite, and the sample mean behaves almost as it would under
independence.

**Long memory:** the correlation decays slowly enough that the sum diverges. Each individual
correlation is small, but there are so many of them that their total is unbounded. The past
influences the present, and its total influence never settles.

The distinction matters because it is exactly the line between a world where the standard
statistical machinery works and one where it does not. Under long memory the variance of the
sample mean does not shrink at the usual rate, so confidence intervals computed the usual way are
too narrow, and the error in a historical estimate decays more slowly than an analyst expects.

That is the deep reason the reservoir needed to be bigger than the standard calculation suggested.
The engineer's problem and the statistician's problem were the same problem.

## The R/S statistic, and its small-sample problem

The statistic is worth describing precisely, because its construction determines its biases.

Take a series of length n. Subtract the mean, producing a sequence of departures. Within the whole
series, track the running sum of those departures — the cumulative deviation from the mean at each
point — and record its maximum and its minimum. The difference between them is the range R.

Then divide by the standard deviation S of the original series. That quotient is R/S.

Under independence, R/S grows as the square root of n. If R/S grows faster, the series shows
persistence; slower, anti-persistence. Writing the growth as a power of n gives H, with 1/2 as the
independent case.

Three properties of this construction matter and are often forgotten.

**It is sensitive to short-run correlation.** A single autocorrelated component can inflate the
range without any long-memory structure being present.

**It is sensitive to non-stationarity.** A trend in the mean produces a cumulating sum that grows
faster than the square root, which reads as persistence. This is the most common source of spurious
long memory in applied work.

**It is sensitive to the sample size in a way that does not vanish quickly.** The small-sample
distribution of R/S is far from the asymptotic one, and the correction factors needed are
themselves contentious.

Taqqu and his coauthors examined these sensitivities systematically across the family of standard
estimators [@taqqu1995], and Franzke and coauthors showed that the behaviour changes again under
non-Gaussian data [@franzke2012]. The practical summary is that a point estimate of H from a few
hundred observations is a weak instrument, and the sign of the bias depends on which nuisance is
present.

## The construction: fractional Brownian motion

In 1968, Mandelbrot and Van Ness published a long paper in *SIAM Review* that turned Hurst's
anomaly into an object [@mandelbrotvanness1968]. It is his most cited paper: 7,747 citations
according to OpenAlex, 7,986 according to Semantic Scholar. Both figures are reported here because
they differ and neither is canonical.

The paper does what the other two papers in this part do not: it proceeds by construction. Rather
than looking for a model that fits a dataset, it writes down the properties it wants and then asks
whether anything satisfies them.

The properties are three.

**Self-similarity.** Scaling time by a factor a scales the process by a factor a to the power H.
The shape of the process looks the same at every time resolution.

**Stationary increments.** The distribution of a change over an interval depends only on the length
of the interval, not on where it sits in time.

**Gaussian increments with the right variance.** The variance of an increment over an interval of
length t is proportional to t raised to the power 2H.

Three conditions, one parameter. When H equals 1/2 the third condition reproduces Brownian motion
exactly. For other values of H the result is a different process with the same self-similar
structure.

I have described the standard formulation rather than quoting the paper, because I did not have its
text. The formulation is stable across the literature that uses it; the paper's own presentation,
including its construction of the process as an integral over past noise, is described in the
secondary sources and I have not reproduced it here.

## What H controls

The parameter has three faces, and the bookkeeping is worth doing carefully because the three get
confused.

**Roughness.** Small H gives a jagged path; the path is continuous but almost nowhere
differentiable, and the smaller H is, the rougher it looks. Large H gives something that looks
almost like a smooth trend with noise on top.

**Dimension.** The graph of fractional Brownian motion has a box dimension of 2 − H. At H = 0.5
this gives 1.5, the value for Brownian motion. At H = 0.7 it gives 1.3, smoother. This is the
connection back to the previous chapter: dimension is the same instrument, applied to a time
series instead of a map.

**Memory.** For H above 1/2 the increments are positively correlated: an increase tends to be
followed by an increase. For H below 1/2 they are negatively correlated: an increase tends to be
followed by a decrease. In the first case, which is Hurst's, the correlation decays slowly enough
that its sum diverges. That is the long-memory condition.

So one number carries roughness, dimension, and memory. The convenience is real, and so is the
trap: three properties that are distinct in intuition — how jagged, how space-filling, how
remembering — are locked together by the construction. **A model that forces three concepts to
move together should be suspected whenever the three disagree in the data.**

## Using a grid before it is defined

Part II introduces a two-question device for deciding what to do with a quantity: does it exist,
and can it be estimated? The device is defined formally in Chapter 14. It is used here informally,
because H is the case that motivated it.

**Does H exist?** For the constructed process, yes. H is a parameter of the model, and the model is
well defined. This is not a matter of opinion.

**Can H be estimated from the data at hand?** Often, no, or only weakly. The estimator is biased,
its bias depends on nuisances that are not observable, and two defensible procedures disagree by
more than their nominal error bars.

Combining the two answers puts H in an awkward cell: **the quantity is real and the estimate is
unreliable.** Two responses are available, and the wrong one is the most natural.

The wrong response is to report the point estimate with its nominal standard error, which conveys a
precision that the procedure does not have. The right response is to report bounds, or to report
the disagreement between methods, and to treat the number as a description of the sample window
rather than a property of the process.

This is why the scale-span rule from Chapter 2 generalises. Its content is not the two-orders
threshold. Its content is that **an estimate of a scale-dependent quantity must travel with the
window it came from**, because outside that window it is not an estimate of anything.

## What the tool cost

Here the story turns, and this turn is the reason the chapter belongs in a book about survival
rather than in a book about time series.

Fractional Brownian motion is Gaussian, self-similar, stationary, and has memory. It looks exactly
like what a financial modeller would want, since real markets show persistence in volatility and
long runs in prices. For a period in the 1990s it was used for exactly that.

Then the mathematics caught up with the use.

In 1997, L. C. G. Rogers published a short paper with a title that is hard to misunderstand:
"Arbitrage with Fractional Brownian Motion" [@rogers1997]. The result is that option prices and
hedging arguments built on a fractional Brownian motion model admit arbitrage — a trading strategy
that produces a riskless profit. The paper's significance is that it identifies the structural
reason: for H not equal to 1/2, the process is not a semimartingale, and the entire apparatus of
stochastic integration, including the construction of a risk-neutral measure, is not available.

The reason is worth stating in ordinary language. A semimartingale is a process that can be
decomposed into a drift and a fair game. Long memory is precisely a violation of the fair-game
part: the past carries information about the future. **The informational content of memory is what
makes the model attractive and what makes it impossible to price with standard methods. The
property is not a defect to be patched; it is the source of the difficulty and the reason anyone
wanted the model.**

Two repairs followed, and both are hedges rather than solutions. Cheridito showed that mixing
fractional Brownian motion with ordinary Brownian motion can restore the semimartingale property
under conditions on H [@cheridito2003]. Guasoni showed that with transaction costs, the arbitrage
opportunities in these models are not attainable in practice [@guasoni2006].

Notice what both repairs do. The first buys back the mathematics by diluting the memory. The
second keeps the model and prices the friction. **Neither makes the pure model work, and neither
claims to.**

## Where the tool went instead

The object did not die. It changed departments.

In 1994, a group at Bellcore measured traffic on an Ethernet network and reported that it was
self-similar over a wide range of time scales [@leland1994]. The paper has 5,265 citations
according to OpenAlex. It is the reason network engineers stopped treating traffic as a Poisson
process, and the reason buffer-sizing calculations changed: a Poisson model assumes that bursts are
local and independent, and a self-similar model says that the same burstiness reappears at every
scale.

That finding came from the same mathematical family Hurst's anomaly had produced, applied by people
who were not thinking about rivers or markets.

The second return is stranger. In 2018, a group studying volatility reported that it behaves like a
fractional process with H of order 0.1 [@gatheral2018]. They called it roughness, and the term
stuck. Note what that value means: far below 1/2, in the regime of strong negative correlation —
not long memory but the opposite, a series that zigzags rather than persists.

So the instrument Mandelbrot built to describe persistence came back twenty-five years after his
death carrying a result about anti-persistence in the one quantity he had devoted the most
attention to. The instrument was indifferent to the direction of the answer. That is what a tool
is, as distinct from a claim.

## Estimatability, previewed

One more thing about H and its friends, because it sets up Part II.

Estimating a long-memory parameter is not like estimating a mean. The information about persistence
lives in the correlation structure across scales, and the estimators available disagree with each
other in ways that are systematic rather than random. Taqqu and his coauthors documented this for
the standard methods [@taqqu1995], and Franzke and coauthors later showed the estimators behave
differently again when the data are not Gaussian, which financial and network data never are
[@franzke2012].

There is a further, more interesting problem, and it belongs to 2018. When Gatheral and his
coauthors fitted their rough model, they made a remark with implications well beyond volatility:
standard statistical procedures designed to detect long memory tend to conclude that long memory is
present, even in data generated by a model that does not have it.

**The detection procedure has a bias toward finding the thing it is looking for.** A reader who
wants to know whether a series has long memory is asking a question that the available instruments
answer in the affirmative rather too often.

This is the first appearance in the book of a distinction that Part II will formalise: the
difference between a quantity that does not exist and a quantity that exists but cannot be
estimated reliably. H exists. Whether the H of a given series can be recovered from the data
available is a separate question, and the answer is often no.

## Claim and tool

**The claim** is that natural and financial time series display long memory, describable by a
fractional process with a parameter above one half. The claim is contested. Some of the persistence
measured in financial series may be an artefact of the estimators, and the most careful recent work
in volatility finds the opposite sign.

**The tool** is the construction itself: write down the properties you want, prove that an object
satisfies them, and study its consequences. That move is what produced the most cited paper in the
material this book covers, and it is what made the anomaly productive rather than merely puzzling.

Seen through the book's device: the tool is a Grade II constant. The construction — self-similar
plus stationary increments plus a variance scaling — survives changes of application domain, from
hydrology to network traffic to volatility. The claim attached to it, that a particular series has
a particular H, does not survive a change of estimator.

## Boundary conditions

The construction holds as mathematics. Every failure below is a failure of application.

It fails in finance when used for pricing, because the process is not a semimartingale and the
standard arbitrage arguments do not apply.

It fails in estimation when the sample is short, because the information about persistence is
carried by long-range correlations that a short sample cannot resolve.

It fails in interpretation when H is read as a prediction. Persistence is a statement about the
autocorrelation structure over a population of paths, not about the direction of the next
observation.

And it fails when the three faces of H are treated as independent. Roughness, dimension, and memory
are bound together by the construction; data in which one indicates persistence and another
indicates roughness is evidence against the model, not an invitation to average.

## Why long memory is hard to establish

The statistical tests for long memory are among the least powerful in common use, and the reason is
structural rather than a matter of sample size.

**The property being tested is a limit.** Long memory means that the sum of the autocorrelations
diverges as the lag grows without bound. A finite sample cannot observe a divergence; it can observe
that correlations are still positive at the longest lag examined, which is consistent with long
memory and also with several other things.

**The competing explanations are not exotic.** They are the ordinary features of economic and
geophysical series.

**Non-stationarity.** A series that shifts between two levels a few times in a sample produces
positive autocorrelations at long lags. The pattern is caused by the shifts, not by a slowly decaying
dependence structure, and the two are difficult to separate in any sample of realistic length.

**Regime changes in the variance.** A series whose volatility alternates between high and low periods
generates apparent dependence at long lags. The 2012 work extending the diagnosis to atmospheric
series takes this possibility seriously, which is why it is worth reading alongside the earlier
results rather than as a confirmation of them.

**Aggregation.** Summing a short-memory process over long intervals can produce apparent long memory
at those intervals, an effect documented in the literature rather than a curiosity of it.

**Why the dispute resists resolution.** Because the tests are weak and the alternatives are
plausible, the evidence that survives is not the evidence that a particular exponent was estimated.
It is the evidence about **where the property holds and where it does not**. Volatility series show
long-memory-like behaviour across many markets and periods; return series show less agreement, and
the disagreement is itself a finding.

**What the practitioner should take from it.** Two things. First, a fitted memory parameter is among
the least reliable numbers in this book's material, for the reasons Chapter 5 sets out. Second, the
useful question is not whether long memory is real in general but whether it is present at the scale
that matters for the decision, which is the scale-span rule again and the reason the rule earns its
own chapter.

**The resolution the book adopts.** Not a verdict on the statistical question, which this material
cannot support, but the practical position: where long memory is present, the standard machinery's
confidence intervals understate uncertainty, and where it is absent the machinery is only slightly
conservative. **The asymmetry means that assuming independence is the more expensive error.**

## What the finance literature did with the construction

The debate over fractional Brownian motion in finance is worth following as a case study in how a
mathematical object is received.

**The object.** A Gaussian process whose increments are stationary and whose correlations decay slowly
enough to produce long memory. Defined by its covariance rather than by a mechanistic construction from
simpler ingredients, which is what makes it tractable and what makes its interpretation contested.

**The objection.** A process with long memory has, in the continuous-time limit, enough predictability
to admit arbitrage. This is not a subtlety; it means the object cannot be a model of a traded price
under the standard assumptions.

**The responses, in order.** Restrict the parameter range; add frictions; change the object. Leland's
transaction-cost result and Guasoni's more general treatment show that under broad conditions the
no-arbitrage property is restored once costs are present. **The objection is therefore about the
frictionless limit rather than about the family.**

**What the sequence demonstrates.** A model can be unusable in one setting and useful in another, and
the difference is a property of the setting. The literature's initial verdict — that the process is
unsuitable for prices — was correct for the setting it examined and was generalised too far, in both
directions.

**What a practitioner should carry away.** Two things. A dependence estimate from a long-memory model
is one input among several, and its use requires knowing whether the decision's horizon sits inside the
measured range. And the arbitrage objection is a reminder that a statistical description of a price
series is not a model of a market. **The description can be right while the market is organised in a way
that prevents anyone from trading on it.**

## Memory in a portfolio context

Long memory is usually discussed as a property of a series. Its consequence for a portfolio is where the
practical content lies, and the consequence is about effective sample size.

**The arithmetic.** Where observations are dependent, the variance of the mean is not the variance of a single
observation divided by the count. It is that quantity multiplied by a factor that grows with the strength of
the dependence. **The factor can be large: a strongly persistent series of a thousand observations can carry
the information of fewer than a hundred.**

**Three consequences for practice.**

**Confidence intervals are too narrow.** Every interval computed under an independence assumption is
understated by the square root of that factor. **This is the most cited and least corrected error in applied
work with dependent data.**

**Backtests overstate.** A strategy evaluated on a dependent series has fewer independent observations than
the record suggests, which reduces the evidence in favour of any edge found in it. **The correction is in the
same direction as the one Chapter 24 makes about track-record length, and the two compound.**

**Diversification overstates.** Assets whose fluctuations share a persistent component are less diversifying
than their contemporaneous correlations suggest, because the shared component does not average away.

**What to do. Two steps, both cheap.**

**Estimate the effective sample size** from the autocorrelation structure, using any of the available
adjustments. **The estimate is rough and the correction is large, which is the right trade when an interval
is being computed.**

**Report both the nominal and the effective count.** A reader who sees "one thousand observations, effective
count one hundred and forty" understands the evidence differently from one who sees the first number alone.
**The second number is the one that should appear in the abstract.**

## What a practitioner should do with the dispute

The academic argument over long memory is unresolved. The practical position, and it is a position rather than a
finding, is what this section states.

**The position. Assume dependence.** Where a series shows persistent behaviour, compute as though it does,
because the two errors are asymmetric. **Assuming independence when dependence is present understates
uncertainty and overstates evidence; assuming dependence when it is absent costs a modest widening of
intervals.**

**Three consequences of the position.**

**Intervals widen by the square root of the effective sample ratio.** A series with an effective count a fifth
of its length has intervals roughly twice as wide. **The correction is large enough to change conclusions.**

**Backtest evidence shrinks correspondingly.** The number of independent observations is the currency of
evidence, and the exchange rate is unfavourable.

**Diversification claims weaken.** Correlations among persistent series understate the shared component, which
does not average away.

**What the position does not claim.** That the process has long memory in the technical sense, or that any
particular exponent is correct. **It claims only that the burden of proof sits with the assumption of
independence, because the cost of being wrong about it is asymmetric.**

**How to apply it without an estimate.** Where an estimate of the memory parameter is unavailable, apply a
discount to the effective sample size of a factor between two and five and state the factor as a convention
rather than a measurement. **A crude correction that is disclosed is better than a precise one that is not, and
better than no correction at all.**

**Why a convention is acceptable here.** Because the alternative is a point estimate of a parameter whose
estimators disagree, and the disagreement is the finding the chapter documents. **A disclosed convention is the
honest form of a correction that cannot be estimated reliably.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The full texts of Mandelbrot and Van Ness (1968) and Hurst (1951) were not available. The
description of the construction is the standard formulation used across the literature that cites
those papers; where the book quotes the papers' own words it says so, and it does not quote terms
or parameters attributed to them without a source.

The value of Hurst's exponent is deliberately not given, for the reason stated in the text: the
figure commonly cited, around 0.7, is more reliably attested in the secondary literature than in
the primary record, and this book does not launder numbers through secondary sources.

The results of Rogers, Cheridito and Guasoni are described at the level of their abstracts,
titles, and the citing literature, which is where the claims above come from. Their proofs are not
reproduced or evaluated here.
